utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in the courtroom and also to those who are assisting us just outside the courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. I was informed that the next witness is to be -- witness to be called by the Defence is Victor Vorobev, and that the Defence failed to make an application for translation to Russian today, and by that risked that we would lose another day. I take it that this will not happen again. I also was informed that the witness offered to testify in B/C/S. We'll check whether this is possible. Yes, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would just like to inform the Trial Chamber that on the 4th of December, the Defence provided a submission to the Registry in which it requested an interpreter for the 8th, 9th, and the 10th. The only problem was that there was a mistake in that on Friday the Defence didn't inform the Trial Chamber that they would need an interpreter for Monday too. But we thought that since we had provided a list of the witnesses on time that it would be taken for granted that an interpreter would be necessary for Mr. Vorobev as well. But since during the preparations for Mr. Vorobev I was using B/C/S, Mr. Vorobev agreed with the Defence that we should speak in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I also understood that he wants a Russian interpretation for tomorrow, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So therefore, it's not just agreed upon that the testimony would be in B/C/S. Could the Defence make an application in writing immediately to CLSS for tomorrow so that we have the -- everything on the record that the translation services can work on it so that we solve the problem more easily tomorrow. Is the Defence ready to call Mr. Vorobev?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please escort Mr. Vorobev into the courtroom. Yes, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, while we're waiting for the witness, I thought it might be an opportune moment for me to inform the Defence and the Trial Chamber that with respect to Anatoli Kruk, the Prosecution has completed its searches on him and I know that he's scheduled for the 22nd and 23rd of January, the Prosecution will be ready at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for your information. So that means that there is no objection as far as the time needed for cross-examination, in respect of the time -- the day on which Mr. Kruk will be called.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vorobev, do you understand me in -- do you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can hear you in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: But could the witness's microphone please be put on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, could you please put on the microphones. Yes. I do understand that my words are translated to you in what you call Serbian and what we usually call Bosnian/Serbian/Croatian, or Bosnian/Croatian/Serbian. That's not your mother tongue, I understand. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My mother tongue is Russian, but today I can speak in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it true that you feel that you're mastering that language sufficiently to testify in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have spoken to General Galic's lawyers in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you would have any difficulty during your testimony to understand what is said to you in B/C/S or - and now I'm addressing the interpreters - if the interpreters would have any difficulty in understanding or translating what the witness says in B/C/S, I'd like to be informed immediately. And I can inform both you, Mr. Vorobev, and the interpreters that everything is done at this moment to see whether we can have a Russian interpreter for tomorrow. Mr. Vorobev, before giving testimony in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. And the text will be handed out to you now by the usher in B/C/S, I take it. Mr. Usher -- yes, that's the B/C/S version. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You'll be first examined by counsel for the Defence. Ms. Pilipovic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Vorobev.

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Before I start asking you a series of questions, I would like you to give us your full name, please.

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: My name is Victor Vorobev.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us your date of birth.

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: I was born in 1954 on the 11th of May.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us what your educational background is. What schools have you completed?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: In St. Petersburg, I finished the three-year cadet school, and then I finished a parachute school in 1986. I then finished an academy in Moscow in 1988 with excellent results.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: With such military education, can you tell us where you worked and where you are currently working, after having completed this education.

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: I worked in the former Soviet Union. I worked in Afghanistan for two years. I worked in Yugoslavia for 18 months and in other places where the Russian parachute unit had tasks.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us where you're working now.

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: I'm retired now. I run a business of my own in Moscow.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You told us that you worked in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us in what capacity did you go to Yugoslavia and when?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: I went to Yugoslavia in April 1993 as deputy commander of the Russian Battalion in Klisa, near Vukovar, and Osijek in Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So you're telling us that as deputy commander of the Russian Battalion you went to Vukovar. Was your battalion a battalion which was part of UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: Yes. The battalion was part of UNPROFOR, and it had to perform UNPROFOR tasks.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us as a member of the Russian Battalion and as a member of UNPROFOR you spent a certain period of time in the area of Bosnia and Herzegovina, to be more specific, in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: On the 19th of February, 1994 I arrived with 500 men from the battalion in Vukovar. We arrived in Sarajevo. And I was the commander of the 2nd Russian Battalion in Sarajevo from February to November 1994 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your last answer. You were commander of the 2nd Russian Battalion -- the interpreters have not heard the whole answer, so could you please repeat your answer. You have told us about the period of time you spent in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. On the 18th of February the Russian Battalion in Vukovar had the task from the Russian ministry to go to Sarajevo with 500 men and to deploy itself in Vrace.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So Mr. Vorobev, you are telling us that from the 19th of February, 1994, as commander of the Russian Battalion, which consisted of 500 men, you arrived at Sarajevo in that capacity and you were in the territory that you have called Vrace.

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vorobev, you said you stayed there until the 5th of November, 1994 in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Throughout your stay in Sarajevo as commander of the Russian Battalion, did you have 500 men?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did the composition of the battalion change?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: At the beginning of April, another 300 men came from Russia to the battalion.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vorobev, when you arrived in Sarajevo, can you tell us, as a member of the Russian Battalion and as the commander, under whose command were you?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: The Russian Battalion had to perform UNPROFOR tasks, and it was subordinated to the commander of the Sarajevo sector, General Soubirou.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vorobev, you have told us that your battalion arrived in Sarajevo in the Vrace territory, in the Vrace area. Can you tell us as commander of the battalion what kind of a task did you have?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: As commander of the battalion, my task was to provide security along the demarcation line and security in the zone of responsibility of the battalion which was assigned to me by General Soubirou.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Vorobev, when you tell us that your task was to deploy along the demarcation lines between the warring factions, can you tell us what the length of the demarcation line was along which you were deployed.

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: The length of the demarcation line was about 4 and a half kilometres, and the depth was about -- between 1 and 1 and a half kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how you organised the deployment of your men along the demarcation line. In which manner was this deployment executed?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: We established observation points along the demarcation line. We replaced men from the French Battalion at the observation points and at other points. It was established where it would be possible to see both sides in optimal conditions.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vorobev, have I understood you correctly? You have told us that you replaced three positions with members of the French Battalion and that the other positions were ones that you determined in accordance with your decision as to where visibility was best, visibility of both sides?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how many such observation posts there were along the demarcation line that was secured by your battalion?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: There were 12 observation points along the demarcation line.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us where the command of your staff was, the command of your battalion that was under your command. In which building was it located and where?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: The command of the battalion, the staff, was located in the police school in Vrace.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: At those observation posts - and you have told us that there were 12 of them - how many members of your battalion stayed in one place, in one position?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: Well, usually one platoon would be assigned to one location, and occasionally in some places two platoons.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence has a map which we received from Mr. Vorobev. It has been suggested as Defence Exhibit D85 [as interpreted], and it has been disclosed to the Prosecution. The Defence would like to show Mr. Vorobev this map, but we only have one copy. Perhaps it would be useful to show the witness this map so that he can use it to show us and you and our colleagues from the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, could perhaps the Chamber first get a general impression of the map so that if we look at parts of the map on the ELMO that at least we've seen the whole, so as to know --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Can you please repeat the D number, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it was D85.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D185. 185. Your Honour, it's a number that the Defence gave to the map on the list of exhibits of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence has a colour copy of this map too. It's the original. But it was a problem for us to copy it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, would you please give it some thought whether it will be possible for us to follow your questions on the ELMO rather than on a kind of a board, because one thing is for sure, that what I see, these lines on the small parts of it could be shown on the ELMO. So even from a distance, having looked at the map -- if you go through broad lines, then perhaps it could be better put on a board. If you want to pay attention to details, then perhaps it could be better put on the ELMO. Would you please give it some consideration what would be the best way to inform the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that the area of responsibility of the battalion can also be seen on the ELMO. That might be a better idea, since Mr. Vorobev would point precisely on the map where the positions were, the observation positions on the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll leave it to you. But I ask you to give it some consideration. Could it be please put on the ELMO, the map. And what part, Ms. Pilipovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We just need a section of the map where the area of responsibility has been marked with those thick black lines, the area of responsibility of the battalion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But that as a whole does not fit on the ELMO, does it? What part would you like to more specifically show us?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, what we can do is first discuss with Mr. Vorobev one part. If he can show us the places where the observers were. And then we can go on to another section of the map, because I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... though -- I mean, the only thing I've got to do is --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can start with east, with the east of the map.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vorobev, could you tell us, on this section of the map that we can see on the ELMO what is first of all marked by these black lines?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: With these black lines -- what is marked with the black lines is the area of responsibility of the battalion, and these black dots, these are the observation posts.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us which observation post is that? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: This is observation post -- the first one, number 1. First there is an observation point located at the Vidikovac restaurant. This is where we replaced the French Platoon. This is where we placed our own platoon, number 5 and number 4, here.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If we look at the map in this section, in this part, we can see only one observation post in this area.

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before continuing, would you please for the sake of the record explain where the witness pointed at when he was referring to the observation post, at which the --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- Replaced the French Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. On the map, the witness indicated the black lines as being the lines marking the area of responsibility of the battalion in that part -- in that part of the city. On the right-hand side in the middle between the demarcation lines he indicated a point as being an observation point. He indicated a dot as being observation post, as being Vidikovac Restaurant, which is what it says on the map. And the witness explained that this was observation post which used to be a position of the members of the French Battalion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we please zoom in on the restaurant, because you say it reads the restaurant. But I am totally unable to read whatever. Could we zoom in on that part so that we can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now I see that the reference to Vidikovac restaurant is a very good one. But we couldn't read it before. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vorobev, if we go towards the west on your map --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to ask the usher, please, if he can move the map now.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vorobev, can you tell us if this observation post that we called Vidikovac Restaurant, did this observation post have its own sign or a symbol?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: We also had the observation post number 3. That was the Jewish cemetery.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, before he answered the question, what was the point, what was the number of the Vidikovac Restaurant, he pointed to the observation post on the map, observation post number 3.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I go on?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He explained that the number 3 observation post was located above the upper black line as the line of the area of responsibility of the battalion going towards the north and that this point, point number 3, or dot number 3, below which it says "observation post number 3," that this position, this post, was the observation post on the Jewish cemetery, as was explained by the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I will now go on a bit further about the observation post number 3. Mr. Vorobev, did you personally go to the area of the Jewish cemetery where observation post of your battalion was located?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how frequently did you go to this observation post?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: Every week, once or twice perhaps -- no, I didn't go every day.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether at this observation post there were one or two of your platoons.

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: One platoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, this position that we called the Jewish cemetery, how long was the distance between the lines of the warring parties? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: I think it was about 300 metres.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, the Jewish cemetery, what was the position of the lines of the warring parties?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: On one side there was the cemetery, on this side, here. That's where the Bosnian army was positioned. And on the other side of the cemetery was the Serb army was positioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vorobev --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, for the record, Mr. Vorobev explained that the eastern side of the cemetery was under the control of the Bosnian army, as he put it, and that the western side was under the control of the Serb army.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vorobev --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I just ask, Ms. Pilipovic: The witness in my recollection made a rather vague gesture, which I could not identify as clearly east or west. So could we please ask the witness. I got the impression that it was rather more north and south than east and west. But we could ask you. You said at one side of the -- of the cemetery, you said "on this side here," and then you pointed at something, that the Bosnian army was positioned, and at the other side of the cemetery the Serb army was positioned. Could you please tell us in more detail where the Bosnian army was and where the Serbian army was, the Serb army was.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vorobev, on the map can you tell us more precisely -- that is, could you indicate.

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: On this side, on this side, that was the Bosnian army. And on this side was the Serb army.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not clear because of the -- could we perhaps zoom in on the --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vorobev, on the map could you indicate precisely the position on the map which indicates the Jewish cemetery. Can you see that place?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the map could be lowered, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Where the observation post number 3 is.

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In relation to the position that you indicate as being the cemetery, can you tell us on which side or to which side were the positions of the Bosnian army and where the positions of the Serb army, in relation to the cemetery that you are pointing to now.

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: On this side, on this side Bosnian army; on this side Serb army.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the record, the witness points to north-east position as being the Bosnian army position and the south-west area as being the Serb army position in relation to the Jewish cemetery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We wondered whether any marking would be better. But we have enlarged very much at this moment the -- and I know that it's the only map but -- would marking not be a better idea, Ms. Pilipovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, it can be done. Your Honour, then the Defence would submit this as a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are we sure that the witness is holding a black pen? Yes. And is it fine enough? Because I know that the map is a different scale from what we see on the screen now.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vorobev, first of all, can you mark with the pen the positions of the BH army as you indicated them to be in relation to the Jewish cemetery, according to what you said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you do that by very small crosses, so a line consisting of small crosses. And that would then be the BH lines. Do you understand what I mean by "small crosses," to make a line consisting of -- or if you prefer, a dotted line is fine as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is it possible to use just dots?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Dots would be fine.

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please make the line a little thicker, please.

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your leave, the Defence would propose that the witness marks the positions of the Serb army with a full line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vorobev, could you use a straight line in relation to the position of the Jewish cemetery. If you can mark, as you indicated already the positions of the Serb army.

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Vorobev, while we're still in the area of the Jewish cemetery, can you tell us, considering that you've already told us that you went there, whether in this area there was a chapel.

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, where was this chapel?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: Here.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you draw a circle there and put number "1" here.

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: There is here a sign for a chapel. That is for a church here on the map.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you put a circle around it.

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Here it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Vorobev, do you personally know which army or whether was there any -- were there any troops in the area of the chapel.

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: In this area, there was the Bosnian army on the north and the east.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if it is necessary for the record, we can mark as east being the positions of the Bosnian army, as the witness marked it with a dotted line, and we can say that the south-west is where the positions were of the Serb army, that is, of the Army of Republika Srpska, denoted with the full line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you allow me to ask for some clarification, because it's not quite clear to me where exactly the witness located the Jewish cemetery. If we look at the line with which you indicated the Serb positions, the Serb line, would that be outside the cemetery or just at where the cemetery ends? I mean, that line, is that the border of the cemetery, or is it more east from the cemetery, at a certain distance from the cemetery? Could you please point at -- now at the Serb -- at the Serb line you indicated with your hand over the pointer. Do you understand what I mean? The line you've drawn indicating the Serb positions, could you please point at them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is that at the border of the cemetery or is it outside the cemetery? These lines, is it just where the cemetery ends or is it at a certain distance from the cemetery?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a little bit outside of the cemetery. Here now I can't point precisely.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vorobev --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your leave, can we just clarify. If you say "just a little bit outside of the cemetery," in relation to the cemetery, how far were the positions of the Republika Srpska army?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. How far from the cemetery is that line you've just drawn?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is it 50 metres, 100 metres, 200 metres?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 20 metres, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 20 metres. Thank you. And your position is then -- your observation post is -- on this map, as you have marked it now, is closer to the cemetery than the Serb line; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then my last question to clarify issues: The way you have marked the BiH positions, is that in the north the BiH positions were north of the chapel; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But you -- okay. But then please clarify, because the dotted line you've drawn in the north is north from where the chapel is indicated on the map. I saw you marking the positions, I would say, at approximately what I consider to be a road just north of the chapel. But if you say that's not correct, could you then please rectify or explain to us how it was.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the line. This line is the position of the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But the chapel was very close to the army positions, 10 metres and not more than that. And this chapel was under the control of the Bosnian army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you say that although the chapel was just south of the lines, it was under the control of the BiH army.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for your clarification. Please proceed, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vorobev, when you tell us that you went to the place that we called the Jewish cemetery and marked it as such, in the area of the chapel did you personally see members of the Bosnian army?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you tell us that in this area of the Jewish cemetery there was your platoon, there was a platoon of yours, can you tell us whether you received from your platoon or from the platoon commander reports on the situation of the warring parties in this area.

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: Every day the platoon commander reported to my duty officer at the battalion about the positions of the Bosnian army and the Serb army and about the distance between the two armies.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us in these reports that you tell us the platoon commander forwarded to your duty officer, what was written in those reports? Do you remember? What was the content of those reports?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: The content of the report was how many times both sides fired, how many other incidents there were in the area of responsibility of the platoon, in the area of responsibility of the observation post, and about the positions --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the last word of the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vorobev, when you tell us that the content --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Which was the last word of your last answer? You said something like: "In the area of responsibility of the observation post, and about the positions," and the interpreter couldn't catch the last words.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I said was about the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter is unable to understand the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters are having problems understanding the witness because I don't speak Russian, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Are you answering in Russian?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Sorry, the French booth would like to say something. The witness speaks B/C/S but with a sort of a Russian syntax. And since I do not speak Russian, I'm really having problems, whereas my colleagues understand Russian.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us in Serbian what was the content of the report that you received from your commander, platoon commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since we were confronted now for the first time with a linguistic problem, I'd like to inform the parties that a Russian interpreter is expected to arrive at 10.45, and perhaps with the consent of everyone concerned, perhaps we should take the first break a bit earlier so as to -- and perhaps make it a tiny little bit longer so that everyone will stand by at, I would say, twenty minutes to 11.00 so that we could really start at quarter to 11.00 with the assistance of a Russian interpreter. That would be more comfortable for you as well, I take it, Mr. Vorobev, and for the interpreters as well. So we'll adjourn for 35 minutes so that we are all ready to start at 10.45. If the interpreter would not have arrived yet, it might be a tiny little bit later. But if everyone is on standby at 10.40. We'll adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom and also the interpreter. Yes, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, until the witness appears, the Defence would like to thank the interpretation service for having ensured that the interpreter could be present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And also the -- yes, I fully support your thanks, and the Chamber does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, before we continue, the interpreter present - and I'd like him to confirm that - is employed by the Tribunal and has made a solemn declaration at the beginning of his services. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes. I am a member of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So therefore, there's no need to ask the interpreter to make a solemn declaration according to the Rules. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vorobev, before we had the break, we were discussing the contents of the report which you would receive from the commander of your platoon through the communications officer in your battalion. So the contents of the report from the observation post 3 area. And that is the Jewish cemetery area. Can you tell us what the contents of those reports was?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: The following was included in the daily reports: Commander of platoon reported on the violation of the cease-fire agreement by both sides and also reported on the intensity of fire coming from the both sides. Also, the deployment of the warring sides' troops and other problems that were encountered within the platoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vorobev, as you told us that you received reports on violations of the agreement between the warring factions and under item 2 you said on the intensity of fire on both sides, can you tell us whether you were personally able to assess how often the agreement was violated? How frequent was this? And when I say "frequent," I mean in a week. How many times did such violations occur every week?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: In the Jewish cemetery area, it was a daily occurrence.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, and did you have any personal knowledge of this when you went there, as to the intensity of fire on both sides? Could you tell us whether the intensity was the same all the time or did it vary in the course of a week, let's say?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: It varied. The intensity was less during day, and the fire was more intense during the night.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vorobev, you told us that you had 12 observation posts. Before pointing out the areas to us on the map, on the basis of what you can remember and given the time you spent there, can you tell us whether there were certain positions, with regard to those 12 positions, where the firing was most intense, on the basis of the reports that you received?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: The fire was most intense in the area of the Jewish cemetery, where there was the post number 3, as well as in the Grbavica stadium area, post number 5, and in the Mojmilo area, post number 9. Mojmilo is here.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the transcript, Your Honour, the witness pointed to a position which is beneath the Grbavica stadium, north of the stadium. This was under number 5, and between the stadium and the line of the battalion positions. And under number 9 he designated an observation post where he said the fighting was most intense in that area. Observation post number 9 is beneath the Russian Battalion's line, beneath the line and the word "Bogusevac".

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vorobev, you told us that your battalion was organised in such a way that you had observation posts and you told us that there were 12 of them, and you have explained to us how many soldiers there were at each observation post. Apart from this manner of organising the deployment of your men at the lines of demarcation, and apart from this manner of receiving reports, can you tell us whether your soldiers were deployed in some other way and whether they covered the territory of the zone of responsibility of your battalion, and could you get reports from them in these areas, in the area of the zone of responsibility of your battalion?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: Can you please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Apart from this manner in which your men were deployed at observation posts, was there some other way that you would deploy your men in the zone of responsibility of your battalion from whom you could gain or obtain reports in the zone of responsibility of your battalion?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: In addition to observation posts in the zone of responsibility of the battalion, there was also a mobile patrol. We had two armoured vehicles that covered the entire area of responsibility and provided information that they collected as they patrolled. The information was supplied either to the duty officer or to me directly.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Vorobev, you've told us about observation post number 3 and you said that you received daily reports on the situation in that area where you observed. Can you confirm that with regard to all the other observation posts that you covered in your zone of responsibility, can you confirm that you received reports in the same way?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what the contents of the reports that you received from other observation posts was?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: It was similar to the content that I described before, the one received from the third post. Violations of the cease-fire agreement, intensity of fire, if there was such, and also if there were any other incidents in the area covered by that post, as well as the situation and problems within the unit itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You told us that the reports that you received from your observation posts, the daily reports that you received, mentioned incidents. Can you tell us what kind of incidents were concerned. On the basis of your recollection, can you tell us what sort of incidents were specified in those reports?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: If in the area of the observation posts there were any incidents of movement of the troops of the warring sides, then that would be reported. I can give you an example: At the observation post number 5, in the northern area of Grbavica stadium, there was a case when from the Muslim side a man moved to the area occupied by the Serb forces. He was either trying to flee or he was wounded, and he ended up being wounded and we evacuated him in our armoured vehicle to the area covered by our observation post. Following that, he was transferred to the military observers. And I don't know what happened to him afterwards. I was immediately informed about this incident by the commander of the observation post number 5.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vorobev, when you received such reports about certain specific incidents, did you react when such incidents occurred and did you talk to representatives of the warring sides?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us whom you met from the warring sides. Which representatives of the warring sides did you meet?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: As a general rule, every week either on Thursday or Friday I or my chief of staff would meet with commander of the 1st Sarajevo Brigade, Veljko Stojanovic. He was from the Serb side. In addition to that, my chief of staff would meet with the chief of staff of the brigade which was positioned across from the zone of responsibility of our battalion. He was a representative of the Muslim side. Unfortunately, these meetings were not very frequent. However, we would meet from time to time. And during those meetings, we would express our protest to both sides concerning violations of the cease-fire agreement.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you tell us that these meetings between representatives of the warring sides, when you tell us that these meetings did not occur frequently and that they were meetings that you had with commanders of the brigades or with chiefs of staffs, and when you say that you lodged protests with them about violations of the truth, at those meetings between the warring sides did you receive protests and what were the contents of the protests?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: I did not receive such protests.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vorobev, at the beginning of our discussion you said that you were subordinated to the sector chief, or rather, the sector commander, General Soubirou. Can you tell us whether as commander of the battalion you had meetings -- or rather, who did you report to, if you reported to anyone?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: Every week on Saturday at noon we would arrive at a meeting with General Soubirou in order to report to him. When I say "we," I mean all commanders within the sector. And then we would report to him one by one. We would report about incidents or quantity of incidents of violations of cease-fire agreements. If there were any other incidents, then they would be reported as well. Then we received certain instructions from the sector commander, General Soubirou.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vorobev, you've told us that every week on Saturday all the battalion commanders in the Sarajevo sector had a meeting with the sector commander at which you made your reports. While you were in Sarajevo, can you tell us which battalions were present in the Sarajevo sector area?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: There were two French Battalions, one Egyptian Battalion, the Ukrainian one, a Russian Battalion, and the airport command.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Apart from the commanders of these battalions you have mentioned and the commander of the airport, were any other UN members present at those meetings?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who else was present at those meetings?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: Chief of staff of the sector, deputy commander of the sector, and the head of the military observers.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vorobev, you've told us about the contents of the subject that you discussed at the meeting with Mr. Soubirou. You said that you discussed incidents. Can you tell us what the subject of the discussions was when you discussed incidents, if some of the commanders of battalions was reporting about his area of responsibility. To the best of your recollection, can you be more specific and tell us what the contents of such reports were, the contents of such reports about incidents.

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: These were, generally speaking, reports on the amount of violations of the cease-fire agreement and suggestions about the weaponry that was used. That was either small arms or heavy weapons that were used.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think you have fully answered my question. You spoke about reports about incidents. Could you be a little more specific, a little more precise, and tell us, apart from the fact that there were reports about violations of the truce and about the sort of weapons that were used by the warring factions, but apart from that at any point in time at those meetings were there any reports about incidents in which in certain zones of responsibility of certain battalions a certain number of men were killed? Did they mention who opened fire? Could you be a little more precise. I don't want to lead you. Were there any such specific reports about specific incidents?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you told us that they discussed the weapons from which fire was opened at the meetings, whether these weapons were of a small or of a large calibre, did you know what sort of weapons the Republika Srpska army had in the zone of responsibility of your battalion?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: Regarding what?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: With regard to the weapons.

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: I knew that Serbian units were mostly equipped with small arms, artillery, and anti-air weaponry that were taken outside of the 20-kilometre zone. We controlled the situation in our area of responsibility. Other equipment and heavy weaponry were all kept in the Lukavica area. The only other case that I saw was a non-operational tank in Dobrinja. It was covered and did not open fire. That was on the Serb side. On the Bosnian side --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I wanted to ask you whether you had any information about the deployment of the BH army's weapons.

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: No. The only thing I knew was that Muslim units also had small firearms. But we assumed that they had 82-millimetre mortars, because there were these exchanges of fire in the area of the battalion.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the interpreter in the courtroom needs to be replaced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I just seek confirmation of the newly arrived interpreter that she has made the solemn declaration at the beginning of her services for the Tribunal and that she's employed by the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I have, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That being confirmed, please proceed, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vorobev, when you answered my question about whether you had any information concerning the weaponry available to the BH army, you told me, I think, that you knew that they had 82-millimetre mortars and that you had established that in situations when fire would be exchanged. Did I understand your answer well?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: Yes, you did.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you said "exchange of fire," can you tell us how often was there such an exchange of fire between the warring parties in your battalion's area of responsibility? Can you tell us that? How frequent was it?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: It happened every day, except that the intensity varied.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you told us that in your view it happened every day but that the intensity varied, were you able to identify the places from which the warring parties acted with regard to the exchange of fire? Are you able to identify the source of fire of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: Not always.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say "not always," it means that on some occasions you were able to do that.

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether you recall such a situation when you were able to determine the direction.

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: Well, let's say when the battalion's headquarters was hit by a shell of, I think, 82 millimetres and it exploded on the asphalt in front of the control checkpoint of the battalion. On the -- the traces and the asphalt and the fragment showed that the shell had passed from the OP5 from the Muslim side, because all the fragments flew southward. In other instances, when there was fire in the immediate area of the observation posts, my subordinates were able to see from which buildings the fire came from the Muslim side and not as frequently they could also see where the fire came from the Serb side, because basically, basically in the area of the observation posts of our battalion the Serbs used private houses.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vorobev. Can you tell us if you remember when, when you told us about the incident when a shell hit the place where your battalion was quartered, could you place it in time?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: It was in May. I do not remember the exact date. In May 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you spoke about the actions from the positions of the Army of Republika Srpska, can you tell us whether in your battalion's area of responsibility you were -- did you know the military formations in the brigade which was in that area, since you told us that you had spoken with the brigade commander? Do you know how many battalions were there in that brigade?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: In the battalion's area of responsibility, there were three battalions of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you personally know where the command posts of the brigade and the battalions, in your battalion's area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: I knew where the headquarters of the 1st Sarajevo Brigade was, where the headquarters of the adversary Bosniak Brigade was and I also knew where the headquarters of the 3rd Battalion of the 1st Sarajevo Brigade was. Because it was in the immediate vicinity of the headquarters of our battalion. The locations of the battalions of the Muslim brigade was not known to me, not precisely, that is.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vorobev, can you tell us, since you said you knew the locations of the brigade and you told us the 1st Battalion too, did you -- can you tell us what kind of buildings were they accommodated in, the battalions and the brigade?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: They were in buildings, in free buildings which were in the territory of their area, the territory of the defence area.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So if I understand you, you tell us that they were in buildings -- what kind of buildings?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: Just ordinary, two- three-storeyed houses.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vorobev, can you tell us, during your time of duty in the area of the city of Sarajevo, did you and how often did you visit the separation lines? First, did you visit the lines which separated the warring parties?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you visit -- I will first ask you about the front line of the Army of Republika Srpska in the area of responsibility of your battalion.

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: How often?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: Personally, once a week. Apart from me, the area of responsibility of the battalion, or rather, the positions at the posts, the posts were checked also by the chief of staff, my deputy, and commanders of companies, so that we checked the situation at our observation post daily to establish the deployment and the positions of the troops of the two warring parties.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vorobev, on such occasions when you visited the front lines and when your sources visited them, did you get some information -- did you personally see the positions of snipers or sniper nests, if I may call them that, in the area of responsibility of your battalion?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: On which side?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you from the positions of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any information whether there were any snipers in the Army of Republika Srpska units?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: As a military man, I assume that there are snipers in every unit, one in a platoon, but in a battalion there would be 27, that is, according to regulations. But depending on the complexity -- on the strength of the battalion, but there could also be a special sniper unit. And I assume that such units existed on both sides as part of the staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you personally see whether on either side --

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vorobev, when you spoke about reports that you received from your platoon commanders or from your operations officers, did you - and you said that you had reports about the violations of the cease-fire, of the agreement - did you ever receive a report that fire had been opened on trams?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say "no," does that mean that during your tour of duty there you never received a report of fire being opened on trams?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Was there any talk at meetings at General Soubirou's when commanders of other battalions were present? Did you hear of any reports during that period of time when you went to those meetings that there had been fire opened on trams?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: During your stay in the territory of the city of Sarajevo, can you tell us if you ever saw soldiers of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what kind of clothes did they wear? Did they have uniforms or what kind of clothes did they wear?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: They had uniforms, but not always, depending, obviously, on supplies. Some of them wore civilian clothes. But they had weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Were you in a position to see soldiers of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what they wore?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: Almost identically. That is, you could find people in civilian clothes under arms and also men in uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you personally move around the part of the city controlled by the BH army?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: Rather often, pretty often, two, three times a week.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you went to that part of the city, can you tell us how long would you stay there, or would you visit some institutions there?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: I went to the headquarters of the Sarajevo sector, where I submitted -- where I reported to General Soubirou. It wasn't only on Saturdays, but if necessary, when either he summoned me or I went to see him, because I had some problems I had to tell him about. At times I met Viktor Andrejev, Mr. Akashi's assistant, Michael Rose, and Michael Rose's command. Several times I visited him. But basically I moved around all the parts of the city of Sarajevo and solved -- and would come across some personal problems or would stop somewhere, stop in a coffee bar to have a cup of coffee or water or something. I also visited other battalions that were stationed in Sarajevo: The French one, the Egyptian one, and the Ukrainian Battalion quite often.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vorobev, now you told us that you went there frequently and that you visited commanders of other battalions. Did you personally, during such meetings with commanders of other battalions, hear or receive any protests, meaning that from the positions of the Army of Republika Srpska some specific buildings in the area of responsibility of their battalion had been targeted?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did they tell you or perhaps submit protests to you concerning the actions of snipers, if I may call them that, from the positions of the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, now the examination will be taken over by my fellow counsel, by my co-counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, good morning. I'd like to go back to what you told us a while ago, and that is your visits to the part of the city which at the time was controlled by the BH forces. You told us that you would stop in a coffee bar or somewhere to have a glass of water, a cup of coffee. And my question is as follows: What was the situation not of a particular coffee bar, but coffee bars around the place, did they -- were they open? Did people patronise them? Were there garden restaurants in summer and so on and so forth? Could you describe to us the coffee bars and other catering establishments in that part of the city of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: I do not know how many coffee bars were in Sarajevo earlier, but in that part of Sarajevo that you are talking about, but at the time when I was there coffee bars and such catering establishments were from the headquarters of the sector to the east part of Sarajevo to Bascarsija, that is the older part of the city. There were quite a few establishments and there were young people there, young and women having coffee, water, smoking, talking. There would also be UNPROFOR members from other battalion, Frenchmen mostly, mostly Frenchmen. Since there were two of them, obviously they were more numerous.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, witness. Now I'd like to go to the period of spring/summer, and I'd like to know whether these coffee bars also had their gardens or their terraces; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: These terraces, would there be people there? I mean, patrons. Would people be sitting there?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, amongst those patrons, I presume there were also distinguished members of the French Battalions and other people, but were there also Sarajevo civilians there?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: Yes, of course, and they were more numerous, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: And those civilians, those civilians who were numerous, what age group would they belong to? Were they young people, less young, elderly, or what?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: They were young people, but I also came across military of the Bosniak army who were on leave and who were taking a break there. But for the most part it was young people.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Could one hear music there also in those -- on those terraces in those gardens?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Did you also patronise such terraces?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Did you have any particular protective measures so as to -- security measures to protect you when you went to those places?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, witness. Do you have the impression that people who were around you were -- and who were patrons of those particular coffee bars, did you have the impression that they lived in fear?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Objection. Calls for speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I respond, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please ask the witness about facts rather than as to impressions on how other people felt.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I will rephrase my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, those persons who were sitting around you, did they show any signs of being afraid; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. And those persons around you, did they show any signs of being happy for being able to attend a social function such as having a drink or sitting in a coffee bar or something else?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: Well, I think it's a personal matter. I cannot be a judge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Witness, my last question concerning this aspect of social life in Sarajevo: Did you see with your own eyes at that time - and I am still talking about the spring of 1994 - did you see very many such gardens and terraces in Sarajevo, relatively many?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President. With respect to the time frame, I don't believe the witness was specifically asked the time frame in which this line of questioning took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have already indicated the time, that is, the spring of 1994. And we know how long the witness was there. And besides, in winter such terraces are not really places to go to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... Summer 1994. But that was already a few lines before, but -- I'll just find it for you. Mr. Mundis, page 36, line 20/21: "Thank you, witness. I'd like to go to the period of spring/summer." And I took it that was the time and the year the witness testified he was in -- he was in Sarajevo, and that was from the 18th of February, 1994 until the 5th of November. Yes. It would have saved time if you would have not interrupted at this moment. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, I'll go back to my question. During the period in question, these garden terraces in Sarajevo, what would you say about them? Did you see many such terraces with people sitting in them and amusing themselves?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: I did see that, yes. People were sitting there and enjoying themselves, and these terraces were quite well visited. However, there were certain places in Sarajevo where I didn't go, so I can't tell you whether there were terraces and cafes there. I believe so, yes, because those areas were even further away from the front line, from the opposing -- warring sides, and based on that I assumed that there were even a greater number of cafes and terraces there too. Had they have been closer to the deployment zones of warring sides, then there wouldn't be as many there. But since this was more to the north, then they were in greater number there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, witness. With regard to the civilians in the town and in the part which was under the control of the BH forces, were you under the impression - and I am now referring to the entire period that you spent in Sarajevo - were you under the impression that when these civilians moved around on foot -- did they show signs of being afraid of Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 17407 to 17413. being targeted? Did they show this in one way or another?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Objection. Calls for speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would like to respond to that. I think that it's possible to know whether people are displaying fear on the basis of their behaviour or if they're not displaying fear on the basis of another form of behaviour. It's not a matter of speculation. This is something that the witness could have seen with his own eyes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you started asking the witness, "Were you under the impression that these were civilians --" it was about an impression. And then you changed to a language, at least in the translation, of did they show signs of being afraid of being targeted, which was a more factual question. Could you tell us, Mr. Vorobev, whether at the period of time indicated by Mr. Piletta-Zanin people moving around, did they show any signs of fear?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: I assume that signs of fear are when people are taking cover and moving from one cover to the other, when they're trying to get a shelter from the fire. These people were walking around freely and enjoying themselves freely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were there any covers you could move from one to another cover? Were there any covers left? Because we heard testimony that certainly in earlier stages there were -- there were covers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is a military term that I used, "taking cover." These people were moving freely. Had they been afraid of anything, they would have walked by the walls of buildings trying to protect themselves. Do you understand what I mean?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I ask you more specifically. We heard testimony of containers being put on crossroads where civilians would pass one side of the containers, presumably because they feared to be targeted if they would choose the other side of the containers. Did -- first of all, did the containers still appear on crossroads?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the most open places, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And would civilians choose both sides of the containers to cross these roads as easily, or would they usually take one side of the containers to pass that crossroad?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, these containers were placed there earlier. I assume that that was done at the time when the fire was most intense. Naturally, a person trying to preserve his or her own life would walk on the side which he or she deemed to be safer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And that was still the same when you were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't understand this exactly. I did see containers, but they were not very numerous.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But where you saw containers, would civilians cross the road indistinctively on the left or on the right-hand side of the container, or would they all choose, or would most of them choose the same side of the containers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They would usually choose the usual side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. One side at least.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Since we've been talking about these containers, witness, do you know if in the area that we call Grbavica, which you're certainly familiar with, do you know whether there were such barricades which had been formed out of containers and other objects of -- or even of screens; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: You don't know or you didn't see such things?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: I didn't see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, I would now like to examine certain other aspects that have more to do with what we call military art. Earlier on you spoke about the fact that the so-called BH army used buildings which were free. My question is as follows: Do you know whether in the part of Sarajevo that was under the control of the Presidency, the premises -- school premises were what you call free, or unoccupied premises; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Do you know whether brigades that were located in the part of the town with many men -- and if they would, which buildings would they be based in?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: As a military man, I assume that they could use vacant barracks, school buildings, and other quite large buildings that were sufficient in order for the troops to be quartered there. I assume that my colleagues from the Ukrainian and French Battalion would know better about this, because they were quartered in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: If we have a civilian building, witness, a school or some other building, a restaurant even, which is located in the town, and there is an ongoing operation there, a military operation is being prepared there, according to the military strategy you are familiar with, is it legitimate or not to target this building, such a building; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President. It's a leading question. It's a hypothetical question. It calls for speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think that this is a leading question, because I have asked the witness to answer by saying yes or no. It's not hypothetical because -- it's not speculative, because the witness spoke about his military experience. And a minute ago the witness said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One of the most well-known features of a leading question is that it can be answered by yes or no. So would you please rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, if we have a military building -- I'll rephrase that question. I think I remember that the question was put to a different witness. If you have a building which was on the ground floor, the first floor of the building, if you have such a building in the city and you have to attack this HQ, this command post, how would you do this if the building is in the city?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: I would use the most accurate weapon in order to destroy the enemy who is located in that building.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. If you don't have direct access or direct view of this target, what kind of weapon would you use?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: Artillery and tanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Isn't it true to say that a tank is a weapon and means which is used for direct fire?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. If it isn't possible to open direct fire because it's physically impossible to do this, what kind of a weapon would you use in such a case?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: Artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: What kind of artillery?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: Howitzers and mortars.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Anything else?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: If I had rocket launchers, I would use them too.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. And if the target is close to the origin of fire, in such a case what kind of a weapon would you use?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: Grenade launcher, and I would aim at the windows of the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, since you've mentioned a grenade launcher, do you know whether this weapon, a mortar, is such that there can be a margin of error?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, margins of error do always exist, whatever you deal with. So would you please try to find the information that might assist us.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll rephrase that question.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And the interpreter in the courtroom needs to be changed again, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I do understand that the -- there will be a change of interpreters. I've understood that before you put your next question to the witness. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Yes, witness, what can you tell us, if you know anything about this, with regard to the age of the ammunition used by both sides in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Objection. Lack of proper foundation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
