utterances.text: Yes. Could you please first find out the basis of the knowledge on which your question relies.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, did you receive or did you have any information during your stay in Sarajevo about the type of weapons used by the forces that were present there and about their ammunition and the quality of that ammunition?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. If you know anything about this, can you tell us what the age of the ammunition used was as a general rule.

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: Both sides used the weapons of the former Yugoslav army, and naturally in the course of a war any weapon can have certain malfunctions that cannot be completely removed. I took your question to mean that any weapon, even the one that functions properly but is used by an incompetent soldier, can result in an inaccurate fire. That depends on a person using -- operating the weapon. So the main factor here is the human one. If a serviceman is competent and well prepared, knows the weapon he's using, knowing its deficiencies, then in order to use it as accurately as possible he will attempt to use precautions and introduce certain other measures. If the serviceman is unprepared, then this can lead to errors and quite serious ones too.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, witness. I would now like you to tell us whether during your stay in Sarajevo you had the opportunity of seeing craters which had been made by such mortar shells. And I am particularly interested in such craters in an asphalt surface or concrete surface.

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you see many such examples?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, did you ever see such mortar shells in Sarajevo where the bottom of the crater was such that the asphalt or concrete had been totally pierced?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: Can you please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I'll repeat that question. We're discussing craters caused by mortar shells, and I'm talking about Sarajevo. During your stay in Sarajevo, did you ever see -- were you ever able to see craters that were such that the asphalt or concrete surface had been totally pierced and it went underground; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: As a military man with 25 years of experience in serving in the army and having participated in many conflicts can say that a mortar shell can never pierce the asphalt surface. In a hard surface, a mortar shell leaves a very small crater. It explodes upon touching the soil. And as far as the asphalt surface is concerned, there can only be a small fragment in the area where the shell landed and in the direction in which the fragments were dispersed, and that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Witness, do you know what a stabiliser is? This is a technical term that we use --

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: My question comes out of your preceding answer. But to make sure that things are clear: This stabiliser, when a shell explodes in a hard -- on a hard surface, asphalt or concrete, on the basis of your experience of 25 years, where will it finish its trajectory? Where will it -- where will the tail fin of the shell end up at the end of its trajectory?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: First of all, witness, could you repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: After the explosion of the shell, the upper part of it explodes and the stabiliser normally flies to one side. I can't tell you exactly which side.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Witness, I would now like to move on to another subject. Could you tell us, when you travelled in the interior of the city under the control of the BH army, did you have the occasion of seeing historical or symbolic monument, buildings such as museums, mosque, or other buildings of such similar symbolic importance?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you mention a few museums that you can remember?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: A museum in Bascarsija area, a mosque in the same area, in the area of the old city.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, with regard to such buildings, museums, and/or mosques, were you able to see whether such buildings had been targeted? Were they systematically targeted and was damage inflicted on them?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you see any other mosques, apart from the one that you mentioned just a minute ago?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: What sort of condition were these mosques in? Could you describe that for the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: How do you want me to describe them?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: The extent of damage, if any, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: Some of them had traces of ricochet. However, I didn't see serious traces of destruction. Those buildings were not pierced by shells and similar. They were bullet-riddled.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, you mentioned ricochets. I would now like to move on to a different series of questions and to talk about small arms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, before doing so, could we have a break now so that -- we had the first break a bit earlier. We'll have a break for 20 minutes, so we'll restart at 25 minutes to 1.00. And Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I've listened carefully to the efficiency. I heard some repetitions. I noticed that you indicated approximately four hours. If there would be a possibility to finish the examination-in-chief this morning, that would be a little bit less than four hours, approximately three hours and a half, but it's not -- I noticed that quite some questions were put twice to the witness, whether he ever saw any crater, it's a question that had been asked already by Ms. Pilipovic. There are other questions. So if also by not -- I heard a lot of repetition of the answers of the witness in the next question. That's not -- usually not necessary. The witness will still remember and without even this confirmation could answer the next question. So if that would be possible, then we could keep pace as we try to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Gladly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll adjourn until twenty-five minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, you may escort the witness into the courtroom. And meanwhile, I would ask the parties whether they have been informed about a change of schedule next week, not this week, because on the 15th - that's the day after tomorrow - we'll sit in the afternoon instead of in the morning, but for next week there is an intention to change the schedule as well, which would mean that on the 22nd of January, the 23rd of January, and the 24th of January - that's Wednesday, Thursday, and Friday - we would sit in the morning and not in the afternoon unless one of the parties, or you, General Galic, would have any objections to this change of schedule. It seems that everyone is nodding no, and for the sake of the transcript --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The Prosecution has no objection to that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The same is true for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only partially, Mr. President, to the extent that for Ms. Pilipovic and myself it's no problem, but next week I'll have to be absent for a day or two. That is the only problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Exactly. No problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So then it will be confirmed, and also it will be confirmed to the Registry that we'll sit on the 22nd, 23rd, and 24th in the morning and not in the afternoon. Then Mr. Piletta-Zanin, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, we were talking before the break and we were talking about shells. But now I'd like to go back to something else. I'd like to move on to something else in order to clarify the situation. You spoke about an attack which came from the part of the city controlled by the BH army, and from your military posts, that is, that the shell fell near your headquarters and it was an 82-millimetre shell. In relation to this fact, do you know whether the agreements concluded between the parties included such weapons but these heavy weaponry, were there such heavy weapons under one of those agreements placed under the UN control?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: A mortar is not a heavy weapon. It is used even as mobile, that is, its base can be carried separately and the mortar itself can be carried separately, so that it can be mobile, it can be moved from one place to the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: During your tour of duty in Sarajevo, did you ever hear the sound of a heavy weapon fired from the Serb area? I'm talking about heavy weapons.

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Now we shall move on to another question, and that is small arms. If an incident happened, wounding people, was it up to your service to establish, to start to conduct investigations of such incidents, of such facts?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: No, that was not part of my duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know if other UN officers were in charge of that, organising investigations?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: There were some units of the military police which were directly engaged in investigating all the events which happened under the UN and all that the UN could know about events taking place in the areas of responsibility of various UN battalions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. And witness, do you know what could one really technically discover during such investigations? What kind of information, technical information, concrete information could be gathered?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I shall be happy to do that. Do you know of your own knowledge what could the investigations establish, generally speaking?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, I'd now like us to concentrate on an incident which you mentioned a while ago, and this is an incident which happened near OP5. You mentioned a person who wanted to cross the line and who seemed to have been wounded in the process. Do you know why or for what reason or by what was -- what kind of weapon wounded that particular person?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like the witness now to focus on the matter of civilians.

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: This man was wounded by a projectile from a small weapon from the Muslim side, from a high-rise building. And he was running in the direction of our post. A small weapon; I hope this was interpreted.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you've come back to this incident, do you know if that person was armed as he was running across the line?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: No. He was not -- he was not armed. He was not carrying any arms, but he had a bullet-proof vest. I cannot say what kind of projectile.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: But do you know if that man was interrogated?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, I'd like now to change the subject and to go back to civilians whom you saw wearing civilian clothes but also under arms. And I wish to precise certain things and not to repeat things. How often -- that is, how often, with what frequency were you able to see with your own eyes such people, such individuals, that is, people wearing civilian clothes but under arms?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: Rather often on both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I want to ask you the following question: In the military theory that you are familiar with, when somebody wears civilian clothes but yet carries openly a weapon, what is that? What is that person?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: Guerilla warriors.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: What does that mean? A soldier, a military?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: It can be a military who does not belong to any army unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Now I'd like to leave that question aside but I'd like to ask you if you ever had an opportunity to personally meet General Galic. And if yes, how many times?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: How many times and what was the frequency of your meetings?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: When he invited me or when I needed to resolve certain problems that fell under his jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, were you ever present at a meeting at which specific detailed protests were made to General -- with General Galic in relation to some incident or whatever?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, when we see a person who was a casualty of a projectile, be it wounded or dead in an urban milieu -- wounded or dead -- how can one establish whether it was the result of a sniper shot and not something else such as, for instance, a ricochet or something else?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President. There's no proper foundation for this type of question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness says that he has 25 years of military experience. Perhaps he knows whether there is a way to draw this distinction, to tell one from the other. I suppose he has personal experience and he certainly knows much more than we do and many others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... Just to find out whether someone knows more than we would expect him to know might not be the proper way of using our time efficiently. But the witness may answer the question whether -- whether you know whether there's any way of establishing whether someone in a urban surrounding being shot would be the victim of a sniper or a stray bullet or a ricochet.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Three seconds to consult my colleague, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And we are now moving on to the last subject, and this will be a general question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, in relation to the buildings and structures generally speaking, was there a difference? And if so, which one, concerning the degree of destruction between the buildings along the confrontation lines and other areas in the city or wherever?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Can you be more precise?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: In the part of Sarajevo that was occupied by Muslim units, there were more high-rise buildings that were destroyed in the early days of the conflict. In the Serb part of Sarajevo were more private houses, which some of them were also destroyed during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, but my question had to do with a possible difference between the front line, that is, the separation line itself, and areas further away from that line in the city. Was there a difference between them? Were you able to see that and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: That is, so what was the situation in areas that were further away from the battlefield strictly speaking, from the front line?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: Well, that area was better preserved. There were no destroyed buildings. There were buildings scarred by ricochets or by bullets, by rounds of fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness - and we have only two questions more, and they are as follows and they have to do now with the accused. You knew him as you told us. Did you ever hear General Galic talk to you about a core military plan, the objective of which would be total eradication, total elimination of Muslims. Did you ever hear General Galic speak to you about such a plan at the level of his corps.

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. You who knew him, you who knew General Galic, how -- what would you say of him as a military man?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: He was a well-trained military man, who was cognisant with the situation in the area of operation of his corps and who skilfully commanded his army. But this is my personal subjective view. Presumably, there were his superiors who could assess his abilities, his skill, his work better than I could do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. Mr. Mundis, is it you or Ms. Mahindaratne who is going to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: It's myself, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You will now be examined by counsel for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, let my pick up with where Defence counsel left off. You just told us that in your opinion, "General Galic was a well-trained military man who was conversant with the situation in the area of operation in his corps."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters are sorry, but could the witness's microphone be moved back away from the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will repeat that this is my subjective view.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, upon what facts or observations do you base that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: When I met General Galic, when I was discussing with him problems about the headquarters, about the stationing of my battalion when we arrived and we had to establish, to identify the area of responsibility, that is, when I went to brief him about all this, he obviously was well cognisant with the situation, he also informed where his units were deployed and what they were doing. He was perfectly conversant with the map and, at times, he also issued some orders to his subordinates and they sounded very literate, from my point of view. And that happened in my presence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What do you mean, witness, when you say,"they sounded very literate," do you mean the subordinates who were receiving those orders?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: No, I mean that he was well informed about the situation in the brigades and he was able to issue orders to his-- to commanders under him. It was at the time when I was establishing the area of my battalion, he was talking to them, he was giving them precise instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: When he was giving these orders, was the subordinate to whom the order was directed also present? Or was this over the telephone or radio? How were these orders transmitted?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: They were present.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What was the reaction of the subordinate or subordinates, on receiving these orders?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: At times, they requested additional information as to what they were being told to do, concerning cooperation with my battalion and rather with me. So they would issued with some other assignments by General Galic. I didn't delve into that but simply from my point of view, it was done in a normal army language.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Approximately what date was this when you had this first meeting with General Galic?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: The 20th of February.

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You told us that he informed you where his units were deployed and what they were doing. Do you recall what he told you with respect to what his units were doing?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: Well, he informed me in general terms about what was being done, that the area of responsibility of the -- that in the area of responsibility of the battalion they were in the defence area, or rather, in the area where the 1st Sarajevo Brigade was deployed, Commander Veljko Stojanovic, and he told me that I had to cooperate directly with him when establishing my posts, that is, the commander of the 1st Sarajevo Brigade should be cooperative in helping me to deploy my observation posts and that he should ensure a coordination with brigade units, that is, with battalions of the 1st Sarajevo Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Other than this meeting on 20 February 1994, approximately how many other meetings did you have with General Galic?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: Seven, eight, I think. Not more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall the approximate date or time period when the last meeting that you had with General Galic was?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: I think that it was in June or July perhaps, at the time when he was about to leave for Banja Luka. I think he was retired then.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Sorry, could we have a short break for the interpreters in the courtroom to change.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: On the seven or eight occasions that you met with General Galic between February and June or July 1994, can you please inform the Trial Chamber how those meetings were scheduled.

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: As a general rule, it was done in direct contact. Either I would come to him and we would agree on that, or we would come -- that would be through the commander of the 1st Brigade, Aca Petrovic, who was in the vicinity of his headquarters. So that was normally done through the commander of the battalion of the 1st Sarajevo Brigade, who was in the immediate vicinity of my headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: On these occasions when you met with General Galic, were the other battalions under sector Sarajevo command also invited, or were these simply meetings between yourself and General Galic?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: In addition to that, there were military observers who were also in the area of responsibility of the battalion. They were also present at those meetings. Occasionally they would meet just the two of them. For example, I would arrive, and in addition to General Galic, there would be somebody else from his headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall the names of any of the other people from his headquarters that you met with?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: Yes. Lugonja -- Cedo Lugonja [as interpreted]. I think that's all. I think that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know what position or post Cedo Lugonja held at the time you met with him?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: Cedo and Lugonja are two people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. With respect to Cedo, what position did he hold at the time you met with him?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: I think that he was lieutenant colonel or colonel, head of artillery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You've just told us that this individual was to your recollection head of artillery. Would that be head of artillery for the Sarajevo Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The individual Lugonja, do you recall what his position or specific post was at the time that you met with him?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall the contents of your discussion with the head of artillery for the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: I did not have discussions with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me try to clarify. Did you have any meetings with General Galic at which he was present?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, do you recall on these seven or eight occasions that you met with General Galic what the subject of conversation was when you met with him?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: Not all of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall in general terms the issues that were discussed?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: I remember the first meeting. In addition to having to coordinate with the commander of the 1st Sarajevo Brigade concerning the deployment of observation posts, so that they wouldn't be in the way of units of the Sarajevo Brigade. In addition to that, I had a number of daily issues, and the accommodation was not ready for the troops. We didn't have mattresses. There were no shower facilities and so on. So I went to the director of -- to the head of the corps asking him to help us as much as he could, and he did, in terms of creating everything we needed for daily needs. So these were the issues discussed at the first meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall any of the topics that were discussed at subsequent meetings?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: Yes, but not all of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you perhaps indicate those issues of discussion that you do recall.

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you please give us some examples of these issues.

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: In June of 1994, additional equipment was delivered to the battalion and it needed to be delivered in Zvornik area, which was the point where the goods entered from Serbia. I had to coordinate the issue of the transfer of this new equipment through positions and posts held by his corps, and this needed to be delivered to the area where the battalion was moved out. And there were several issues that needed to be resolved concerning the transfer through the checkpoints, so that the units of the corps all had information that the Russian Battalion would be passing through with the new equipment to the area where the battalion was located in Vrace.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Once this issue was raised with General Galic, did you encounter any difficulties in getting your equipment through these checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: On any of the occasions that General Galic met with you, did he ever complain to you about protests involving shelling that he received from any other UN personnel in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: On any of the occasions that General Galic met with you, did he ever complain to you about protests involving sniping that he had received from any other UN personnel in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, what was your rank at the time you were in Sarajevo, from February 1994 onwards?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Where did these meetings that you attended with General Galic take place?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: On the 20th of February, 1994 the meeting was held in the area of deployment of the battalion at the police school. He listened to our problems and promised to help. The following meetings were mostly held at the headquarters of the corps in Lukavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So on the first meeting he actually came to the police school to meet with you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: Yes. It wasn't only him. General Soubirou came as well, as did other officers of the UN sector headquarters. In addition to them, there were also some leaders of the Serbian army that was deployed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall who these leaders of the Serbian army that were deployed there, do you recall the names of any of those individuals?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you please indicate the ones that you do recall.

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: Veljko Stojanovic, commander of the 1st Sarajevo Brigade; Aca Petrovic, commander of one of the battalions within the 1st Sarajevo Brigade, which was located immediately in the area of our battalion. His command post was in the immediate vicinity of our battalion, within some 50 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Other than the meetings that took place at the police school in Vrace and at the corps headquarters at Lukavica, did you ever meet with General Galic at any other location?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, can you tell us a little bit more about the military training that you had and experience that you had. Did you have a specialisation -- I know you told us you had parachute training. Did you have a military specialisation in the Russian army?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: I went through all levels of military training that exist within the Russian army. I completed military school in St. Petersburg, then high military school in Rjazin and airborne school. After having spent two years in Afghanistan, I completed the military academy called Frunze, which lasted for three years and is the highest institution of that nature. And I became an officer of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you have command experience in the infantry?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: During 25 years of my military service, I always was in command of parachute units, starting with the platoon and ending with the regiment. So one can say that I had experience with infantry, because parachute units end up fighting as infantry. The only difference is that air assault units have special tasks in addition to those had by infantry, because they are supposed to enter the rear of the enemy and destabilise the enemy troops there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Earlier you told us, witness, that one of the main factors in the soldiering profession is a human one, which goes towards the level of training that individual soldiers have.

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do commanding officers have specific duties with respect to training of their soldiers?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do commanding officers have a responsibility and a duty to know the level of training that their soldiers have?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: Yes. Each at their own level.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So that one would expect a company commander to have a more thorough knowledge of the specific training and capabilities of his individual soldiers?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: Companies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You would expect a company commander to have a more thorough knowledge of his individual soldiers' capabilities than a battalion commander; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: In your 25 years in the Russian army, did there ever come a situation in which your superiors ordered your unit to undertake a military operation that you did not personally think your soldiers were capable of undertaking?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This only concerns the private life of the witness and certainly not the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It seems to be professional life, but the relevance issue, Mr. Mundis, I don't know whether it could be discussed in the presence of the witness, but is it -- are these questions of a rather theoretical nature or ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution position is that it goes to demonstrating the duties and responsibilities of a commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But -- I'll allow you this one question and then -- these are rather general issues as far as I understand them at this very moment. So would you please answer the question put to you, that was that -- whether you ever were in a position where you thought your subordinates could not -- that you thought your soldiers were not capable of undertaking an order that was given to you by your superiors.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will not answer that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you give us the reasons why you would not answer that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is my personal experience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because this has to do with my personal experience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But you're sitting here to testify about your personal experience. I mean, nothing else is at stake then -- so I would please invite you to answer the question. I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My experience in Yugoslavia, but not the experience gained elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have to contradict that. Your experience, you have testified, for example, about your training, et cetera. So you're now asked about your experience. I don't think that Mr. Mundis will ask you any further details as to where and when - Mr. Mundis - so no one will ask you -- the question is just whether you ever experienced that you thought that your soldiers were not capable of undertaking an order you received. Would you please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: In a situation like that, witness, does a commander have any obligations with respect to the superiors?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Mr. President. The question is too vague, the one that has to do with obligation towards the superiors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I perhaps put the question in a different form to you, Mr. Vorobev: What do you think a commander should do under such circumstances?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Everything he can in order to execute the task.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And has he any duty in respect of his superiors, apart from trying to do what he thinks his soldiers are not capable to do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He has to show initiative, a reasonable one, in order to execute the assignment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand. But if a commander thinks that is his soldiers are not capable of executing the orders given to the commander, is there any duty for the commander to his superiors? Should he inform them? Should he advise them? Should he -- what -- would there be anything he should do apart from --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand what you are saying, but naturally when he receives an assignment, he needs to seek all the necessary explanation. If he's unable to carry it out, he must report to the higher standing superior that he needs either additional forces or something else if he is to carry out that order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, witness, during your career in the Russian army, units that you commanded had training on various types of mortar systems.

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: The troops -- the assault troops also include mortar artillery, mortar units. But it is a matter of military organisation and the structure of the staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you have any professional training or experience dealing with mortars?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you have any professional training or experience in using mortars with delayed fuses?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, isn't it right that the purpose behind using a delayed fuse is so that the mortar will not explode upon impact with the ground or other surface?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What in your view, witness, is the purpose of using a delayed fuse?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: Additional charge, supplementary charges placed in the mine. And the delayed fuse ensures that the -- that the shell will fly further in order to preserve the gun powder charge and the shell has to fly further. That is the purpose of the delayed fuse.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, what is the purpose of a fuse in a mortar?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: Well, it is a professional matter for a gunner, for an artillery man. My task is to tell the gunner the target, and he then decides what else needs to be done. This is a question for experts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I take it from that answer, witness, that this discussion is beyond your military expertise?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, on several occasions earlier this morning --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask one thing. Mr. Vorobev, you have been asked about delayed fuse, fuses. Would your answer -- do you understand to be delayed fuses the same as time fuses, or would your answers have been different if you would have been asked about time fuses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot give you an exact answer. I know that supplementary charge is placed on the shell before it is ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, on several occasions earlier today you talked about UN military observers. Was the Russian Battalion at the time you commanded that battalion part of the UN military observer chain of command?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you have at the time of your arrival any briefings in which it was explained to you what the purpose of military observers in Sarajevo were?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: Generally speaking, at all meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Part of the duties and responsibilities of the military observers was to lodge protests with the parties; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: I wouldn't know. Perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: But as the battalion commander of the Russian Battalion, your duties and responsibilities did not include lodging protests, did they?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: On how many occasions did you lodge oral protests with either of the parties?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: At every meeting, at every briefing we would discuss problems that had taken place, the problem of exchanges of fire between the warring parties. I mean, we met with the brigade commanders once a week of the two parties and we discussed those matters, that is, established the intensity of fire, who started the first one, who responded. But it wasn't a protest. Those were discussions, and we were trying to get the warring parties to comply with the cease-fire agreements.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, what would you characterise as being a protest? If these complaints or discussions weren't protests, what was a protest?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: Well, a protest means concrete facts that have taken place and concrete results following the investigation of a primary fact. That is, one needs to indicate the number of shots, the number of casualties. That is how I understand a protest. And in the daily reports to the sector staff, we would establish this situation in the area of responsibility for the sector commander, the places of the most intensive exchanges of fire between the two sides, the duration of the exchange of fire, and the positions of the troops -- of one's own troops in the areas of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And was this information that you just described which was contained in the daily reports to the sector staff also relayed to the parties?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: When you had meetings with either of the parties, what type of information did you relay to them?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: We focussed our attention on the fact that especially in the areas of responsibility of some OPs there was quite intensive fire, and we were trying to make the commanders of relevant brigades to ensure that they see to the compliance with cease-fire agreement. We were drawing their attention to the fact that agreements need to be observed and they should stop firing at each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: This information was conveyed by yourself personally to each of the sides that were operating in the vicinity of your area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: I already said that every week we would meet with the brigade commander, or rather, commanders of the Serb and the adversary, either myself or my deputy, and we would inform them about facts, that is, about the violations of the cease-fire agreement, which had taken place during the preceding week. That is, how many times, where and near which of the observation posts had this gunfire taken place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did these meetings that you had on a weekly basis have any noticeable effect on the conduct of the hostilities in your area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: Generally speaking, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you elaborate for us what that effort was, what you noticed changed as a result of these meetings?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: Well, to begin with, the intensity of fire changed. That is, it abated. And I say that in June and July and, I'd say, in August and on the gunfire was -- the exchanges of fire grew less intensive. But that was over a period of time in the area of Sarajevo. There were no more casualties, at least to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I have a couple of questions regarding the map before we break for the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: If the registrar could assist me with the number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. How much time would it take, because we have one minute left, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: One minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One minute. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, with respect to the map D185, which is to your right on the ELMO, do you recall approximately when the markings, other than the markings that you made today -- the markings on that map, do you know when they were made?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: You mean the area of responsibility and the location of observation posts?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: It was done in February 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The indications by the various observation posts where it says, for example, "OP1" or "OP3," can you tell me why the "OP" is made in Latin letters rather than Cyrillic letters, which seems to be the case with respect to all the other markings?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: Because this acronym was adopted. All the markings, they were the ones that were adopted by the UN forces and are the same throughout. So observation post is called OP, and we used the same, and then the number. Battalion, you can see it's marking its abbreviation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I understand that, but --

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV
utterances.text: Patrol, you see the patrol route, APC route.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: My question wasn't so much why the "OP" but simply why the "O" and the "P" were made in the Latin alphabet rather than the Cyrillic alphabet --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Even if we're interested now in the linguistic question, I really fail to see the relevance of this question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis, I take it that you want to explore the way the map was created or ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: That could be part of it, Mr. President. It's quite striking that all the markings are in Cyrillic with the exception of that one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So -- Mr. Vorobev, could you please answer the question. The question was about why when marking on that map an observation post Latin letters were used, whereas a lot of other marks are made in Cyrillic. So we're not talking about whether you should use a "P" or not a "P," but why you should write the "P" as the Latin "P" rather than a Cyrillic "P."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean that everything else is in Russian? Well, it's simply that it was easier. It was easier for us to do it this way. Everything else that concerns technical markings, observation posts or battalion locations, it was all marked as laid down by the rules of the UN forces. I don't think that the French would put these particular markings in their language, the names of their own units or various settlements, where perhaps if it says "russe," but in Russian I don't see why that is a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, there's no problem. But there's the difference, a use of letters, where part of the markings are made in Cyrillic letters, where an observation post is marked, there the Latin letters are used. May I ask you, "OP," who has marked that on the map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The head -- the chief of my staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I think that's all for today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Questions have been put to the witness. Questions have now been answered. Mr. Vorobev, this concludes your testimony, but just for today. We'll continue tomorrow morning at 9.00 in this same courtroom. May I instruct you not to speak with anyone about the testimony given or still to be given tomorrow. So you don't speak about it, not with anyone, friends, parties, whoever. And we'd like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.00. Yes. Then we'll adjourn until --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But could the usher -- unless there's any reason that the witness should stay present.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a simple matter of organisation. Since we shall obviously need the interpreters -- Russian interpreters for tomorrow. But we should also like to know how long will the Prosecution need to still cross-examine this witness tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I would not expect to need more than about one hour in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That would stay certainly within the limits of the examination-in-chief. We'll adjourn until tomorrow morning at 9.00, unless Mr. Mundis, you have -- okay. We'll adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
